introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. History 2 (0560), Paper 2 - Modern World History Since 1870, ORDINARY LEVEL, June 2026. Duration: two and a half hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FOUR Questions. TWO questions must be chosen from SECTION A, ONE from SECTION B and ONE other from SECTION C. One of the two questions chosen from SECTION A must be a Starred question (1A\* or 1B\*). Maps should be used to illustrate answers where appropriate. All questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION A - CAMEROON SINCE 1850.** Question One is compulsory. Answer TWO questions from this section. Answer 1A\* or 1B\* and any other question from this section.

**1A\* (Starred question)**

Study this extract on the scramble for Cameroon from 1850 to the 1880s and then answer questions (a-e) which follow. (The maximum mark for each sub-question is indicated in the brackets.)

> Trade competition and rivalry between the various European powers sparked off the scramble and later the annexation of Cameroon. In the 1840s, Britain had successfully signed anti-slave trade, friendship and commercial treaties with coastal chiefs which appealed for legitimate trade.
>
> In order to consolidate these gains, she established trading companies and monopolised trade on the coast. British monopoly of trade, however, did not last for long as after 1860 British traders faced competition **[line 5]** from the Germans. In 1868 the German traders established another trading firm also. Keen competition between German and British traders led to rivalry, thus pushing the Germans to employ other measures to dominate trade. French traders on their part were active in the south - eastern coast. They opened trading stations and were moving towards Douala, signing secret treaties with local chiefs...between 1860s and early 1880s the local Duala chiefs and kings addressed letters to the British government requesting for **[line 10]** annexation.
>
> Although the British colonial office was opposed to the annexation of Cameroon, by 1882 the British decided to enter the race. In May 1884, the British Consul was sent to create a floating consulate with authority over the coast from Nigeria to Cameroon and to sign treaties with the local chiefs. Hewett only arrived on 19th July after the ...Treaty had been signed and Cameroon annexed by the Germans. ...therefore **[line 15]** arrived 'too late'. The British refused to recognise the ...Treaty.

*Source: Tazifor Tajoche: Cameroon History in the 19th and 20th Centuries.*

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) (i) Apart from Britain mentioned in line 2, name **two** other European powers actively involved in trading activities along the Cameroon coast.
(ii) Which **two** local chiefs did Britain sign anti-slave trade, friendship and commercial treaties with in the 1840s to encourage legitimate trade? (line 2)

(2+2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Germany and France [1 mark each].** The extract itself names the Germans (lines 5-7) and the French (lines 8-9) as the traders who competed with the British on the coast. (Other European traders, such as the Portuguese and the Dutch, had been on the coast earlier, but Germany and France are the two powers the passage points to.)

**(ii) King Bell and King Akwa [1 mark each].** These were the two leading Duala rulers on the Wouri estuary. They signed the anti-slave-trade and friendship treaty with Britain in 1840 and later treaties on legitimate commerce, in exchange for presents and the promise of British protection of trade.
themes: european trade on the cameroon coast

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) (i) Name any **one** British and **one** German firm involved in trade with Cameroon before 1870. (line 6)
(ii) Give **two** political reasons why the traders of the companies demanded in b(i) above sought assistance from their home governments to dominate trade.
(iii) Apart from Douala, give the name of **one** other coastal town that served as a trading station for these European powers mentioned in a(i) above.

(2+2+1 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) One British firm and one German firm [1 mark each].** British: Hatton and Cookson of Liverpool (also acceptable: Richard and William King, or the Liverpool firms that followed them). German: the Hamburg firm of Carl Woermann (Woermann), which opened a trading factory at Douala in 1868 (line 6 of the extract: "In 1868 the German traders established another trading firm").

**(ii) Any two political reasons [1 mark each].**
1. *To obtain protection of their lives and property.* Traders were in conflict with Duala rulers and rival firms over debts, "trust" (credit) and the "comey" (customs dues), and wanted naval protection (gunboats) and consuls to enforce their claims.
2. *To obtain a monopoly of the trade.* If their own government declared a protectorate or annexed the coast, the firm would enjoy privileges and could shut out rival firms of other nations.
3. *To protect the coast against rival powers.* Each group feared that the other nation's government would take over the territory and favour its own traders, so each wanted its government to act first.
4. *To have disputes with the chiefs settled* by treaties and a government agent instead of private bargaining.

**(iii) Any one town [1 mark].** Kribi (also acceptable: Bimbia, Victoria, Batanga, Campo, Malimba). These were coastal points where firms kept trading stations or hulks for palm oil, palm kernels, ivory and rubber.
themes: european trade on the cameroon coast

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) (i) Name **two** Cameroonian chiefs who addressed letters to European governments requesting for annexation in the 1880s. (line 10)
(ii) What methods did the German traders use to bypass the British?

(2+2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) King Bell and King Akwa [1 mark each].** The Duala kings (Ndumbe Lobe Bell and Dika Mpondo Akwa) wrote to Queen Victoria and to the British government several times between the late 1870s and 1883 asking Britain to annex their territory or to make it a protectorate. (Accept also other Duala rulers who signed such petitions, for example Joss.)

**(ii) Any two methods [2 marks].**
1. *Direct buying from the producers.* The German firms opened factories (trading posts) up the river and in the interior, so that they could buy palm produce from the producers and avoid the Duala and British middlemen.
2. *Offering better terms.* They paid higher prices for produce and sold goods cheaper, and gave generous presents ("dashes") to chiefs.
3. *Making treaties with local rulers who were rivals of the British-friendly chiefs.*
4. *Appealing to their own government.* They asked the German government for gunboats and a protectorate, which led to the arrival of Gustav Nachtigal in 1884.
5. *Using their own steamship line* (the Woermann line) to link Hamburg and the coast regularly and cheaply.
themes: petitions to britain from cameroon coast

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) (i) Which British Consul was sent in 1884 to sign annexation treaties with the Cameroonian coastal chiefs? (line 13)
(ii) What major event had taken place before 19th July 1884 to alter the plans of the personality mentioned in d(i) above?

(1+1 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Edward Hyde Hewett [1 mark].** He was the British Consul for the Bights of Benin and Biafra, sent to Cameroon in 1884 with instructions to sign treaties of protection with the coastal chiefs.

**(ii) The signing of the German-Duala Treaty [1 mark].** On 12 July 1884 Gustav Nachtigal, the German Imperial Commissioner, signed a treaty with the Duala kings (Bell and Akwa), and Germany proclaimed the protectorate of Kamerun a few days later (14 July 1884). Hewett arrived on 19 July, when the Germans had already annexed the coast, so he came "too late" (the blanks in the extract are this treaty).
themes: british consular rule on the cameroon coast

questions.enonce_markdown:
(e) In the text competition and rivalry between European powers was principally around trade;
(i) List **two** trade commodities in your locality that have caused rivalry among the inhabitants.
(ii) State **one** reason for these rivalries.
(iii) Give **two** measures that the local authorities can adopt to reduce the rivalries?

(2+1+2 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
*This question depends on the candidate's own locality; a model answer is given and any valid local example is accepted.*

**(i) Two commodities [1 mark each].** Cocoa and timber (other acceptable examples: coffee, palm oil, cattle, fish, land for food crops).

**(ii) One reason [1 mark].** Competition for the limited land, buyers and markets, because whoever controls the best farms or the best selling points earns the highest profit.

**(iii) Any two measures [1 mark each].**
1. *Dialogue and mediation.* Traditional councils, chiefs and divisional officers can hold meetings to settle disputes over land boundaries and markets peacefully.
2. *Clear rules and regulation of markets.* Fixed market days and places, fair weights and price information, and fines for cheating.
3. *Cooperatives and producer groups,* so that farmers sell together at a fair price and share the profits.
4. *Marking out farm and forest boundaries* with the help of the land authorities, to avoid conflicts over ownership.
themes: local trade rivalry and conflict resolution
